stops.narrative: Distinguish a measuring device, a prescribed document and an excavated record. Follow the people preparing and processing the materials.
Use the map to keep Girnar, Dhauli and Kandahar evidence separate. Name the work an instruction requires and the local evidence needed to test its results.
Inspect the earlier jar, then read the later civic rules. Explain why supplying water or selling goods did not itself grant Assembly participation.

conclusion: Rules needed people and material work. A common standard, a royal instruction and a civic eligibility procedure are different institutions. Explain one mechanism, identify whose experience survives and ask what evidence could test the account.

evidence.prompt: Which comparison respects both institutions and ordinary work?

options.text: Records and objects reveal different tasks and powers; announcements, local practice and political eligibility require separate evidence.
options.feedback: Yes. Identify the rule, the people doing the work and the evidence of implementation. A shared question does not erase differences in status or date.

options.text: Publishing a rule proves that every person experienced its promised result.
options.feedback: A decree or instruction preserves a claim. Local records, material use and people’s experience are needed to investigate its effects.

options.text: Anyone shown working in a public place must have held the same political rights.
options.feedback: Water provision, commerce and Assembly participation were different activities. The jar cannot identify each figure’s legal status or turn public work into universal franchise.
